moment.text: Very soon the Rabbit noticed Alice, as she went hunting about, and called out to her in an angry tone, “Why, Mary Ann, what _are_ you doing out here? Run home this moment, and fetch me a pair of gloves and a fan! Quick, now!” And Alice was so much frightened that she ran off at once in the direction it pointed to, without trying to explain the mistake it had made. “He took me for his housemaid,” she said to herself as she ran. “How surprised he’ll be when he finds out who I am! But I’d better take him his fan and gloves—that is, if I can find them.” As she said this, she came upon a neat little house, on the door of which was a bright brass plate with the name “W. RABBIT,” engraved upon it. She went in without knocking, and hurried upstairs, in great fear lest she should meet the real Mary Ann, and be turned out of the house before she had found the fan and gloves.

previous.text: It was the White Rabbit, trotting slowly back again, and looking anxiously about as it went, as if it had lost something; and she heard it muttering to itself “The Duchess! The Duchess! Oh my dear paws! Oh my fur and whiskers! She’ll get me executed, as sure as ferrets are ferrets! Where _can_ I have dropped them, I wonder?” Alice guessed in a moment that it was looking for the fan and the pair of white kid gloves, and she very good-naturedly began hunting about for them, but they were nowhere to be seen—everything seemed to have changed since her swim in the pool, and the great hall, with the glass table and the little door, had vanished completely.

next.text: “How queer it seems,” Alice said to herself, “to be going messages for a rabbit! I suppose Dinah’ll be sending me on messages next!” And she began fancying the sort of thing that would happen: “‘Miss Alice! Come here directly, and get ready for your walk!’ ‘Coming in a minute, nurse! But I’ve got to see that the mouse doesn’t get out.’ Only I don’t think,” Alice went on, “that they’d let Dinah stop in the house if it began ordering people about like that!”

moment.text: Very soon the Rabbit noticed Alice, as she went hunting about, and called out to her in an angry tone, “Why, Mary Ann, what _are_ you doing out here? PRIORITY RULES:
1) No text or symbols anywhere: no letters, numbers, signage, logos or inscriptions, no writing on labels, bottles, books, signs, slates or playing cards, and no artist's signature or initials in a corner.
2) One scene painted to every edge of the frame: no panels, collage, border, frame, margin, visible paper or blank backdrop, and never a photographed painting or mockup.
3) Nothing from outside the moment's era.
4) Natural anatomy: no extra or malformed limbs, hands or faces.
5) sexually explicit content and lingering gore are never shown; serious depictions of battles, blood and death and non-sexual nudity may be, treated seriously.
6) No likeness of any real actor, performer or public figure.
7) Show the SELECTED CHARACTERS with their canon. Anyone else appears only as an unnamed figure the scene plan describes.
If instructions conflict, follow these rules, then the work brief, then canon, then the art style, then the scene plan. The text decides who is in the scene; canon decides how they look; the scene plan decides this moment's place, time, light, clothing and action. Owner look constraints, when given, are binding.

SCENE: one moment of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland, The Rabbit Sends in a Little Bill ¶2 to The Rabbit Sends in a Little Bill ¶3: "Very soon the Rabbit noticed Alice, as she went hunting about, and called out to her in an angry tone, “Why, Mary Ann, what _are_ you doing out here? Run home this moment, and fetch me a pair of gloves and a fan! Quick, now!” And Alice was so much frightened that she ran off at once in the direction it pointed to, without trying to explain the mistake it had made. “He took me for his housemaid,” she said to herself as she ran. “How surprised he’ll be when he finds out who I am! But I’d better take him his fan and gloves—that is, if I can find them.” As she said this, she came upon a neat little house, on the door of which was a bright brass plate with the name “W. RABBIT,” engraved upon it. She went in without knocking, and hurried upstairs, in great fear lest she should meet the real Mary Ann, and be turned out of the house before she had found the fan and gloves."

WORK BRIEF (alice-in-wonderland; what may be shown; it outranks the style, the look and the plan):
Tone: Whimsical and dreamlike, with a gently unsettling bewilderment that turns to sharp absurdity at court.
Depiction: Alice's changing size reads clearly against doors, furniture, trees and other figures.
Depiction: Talking animals are drawn as animals, with human posture and dress where the text gives it.
Depiction: Playing-card courtiers, gardeners and soldiers are flat, oblong cards with heads, arms and legs.
Depiction: Threats and executions stay threats or slapstick; no gore or real injury.
Depiction: Take no likeness, costume or prop from film or animated adaptations.
Era: Victorian England and its dream Wonderland
People: Alice, a young Victorian English girl, among talking animals, card courtiers and odd Wonderland folk.
Dress: A Victorian child's dress and pinafore for Alice; period robes, waistcoats and hats for others.
Buildings and objects: Riverbank, rabbit-hole, long hall, little door, cottages, mushroom wood, croquet-ground and courtroom.
Technology: Pocket watches, oil lamps, slates and pencils; no machines or modern devices.

SELECTED CHARACTERS: Alice; White Rabbit

CANON (fixed identity of the figures, places and things present; the scene plan decides pose, expression and action):
- Alice: a young Victorian English girl of about seven or eight, slender and small-boned with a child's build, fair skin, long loose hair that falls into her bright eager eyes and is tossed back from her face, and a round, earnest face. She wears a Victorian child's dress with a pinafore over it, with stockings and buttoned shoes on her feet, and carries nothing else of note.
- White Rabbit: an anthropomorphic white rabbit, upright and human-proportioned, with pink eyes, white fur, and a small, anxious build. Dressed in a splendid waistcoat with a pocket holding a pocket watch, often carrying white kid gloves and a large fan, and as herald at court a trumpet and a rolled parchment scroll. Fussy and hurried in manner, with a waistcoat and whiskers as his most distinctive features.
- The White Rabbit's House: a neat small Victorian cottage of warm red brick with a steep slate roof, a narrow chimney and a single small casement window set low in the wall. A bright brass plate engraved W. RABBIT is fixed to the front door, which opens inwards. Inside, a tidy little room has a small table set in the window, a looking-glass on the wall, and a narrow staircase rising to the upper rooms. Rooms are modest in scale, so the house visibly strains around a grown Alice.
- Only Alice, White Rabbit, the White Rabbit's house have this canon look; other selected people get clearly different faces, hair and clothing colours.

ART STYLE: Ink & Watercolor
Rendering: Pen-and-ink drawing with transparent watercolor washes laid over the whole picture; a finished watercolor painting of the work's world, not a sketch.
Negatives: Washes, pigment and scenery must reach every edge. No white or cream paper margins, unpainted corners, paper edges, sketchbook, tape, border or vignette. Do not present the scene on a sheet of paper or against a blank backdrop. Avoid photorealism, digital airbrush smoothness and cartoon caricature.
Palette: Transparent washes of ochre, sienna, indigo and sage covering the whole picture, sky and corners included.
Lighting: Clear natural light; shadows as cool layered washes.
Materials and texture: Confident ink linework, wet-in-wet blooms and granulating pigment within the depicted world.
Composition: A complete scene: setting, sky and ground painted out to every edge and corner, with detail concentrated on key subjects.
